html:
Archaeologists working at Terqa on the Euphrates in Syria found what were identified as cloves in a pottery jar in a house dated to about 1720 BCE. At the time, cloves grew only on a few small islands in the Moluccas of eastern Indonesia, some 10,000 km away.

If the find is right, cloves had crossed half the world by relays of traders long before any written account of such a route. They probably moved by Austronesian sailors through island Southeast Asia, by others across the Indian Ocean to South Asia, and on through the Gulf; compare Indus seals in Mesopotamia. Some scholars doubt the identification, and the routes are guesswork.

Later the record is clearer. Han dynasty courtiers in China chewed cloves to sweeten their breath, and Rome imported them. The clove and nutmeg islands drew the Portuguese and then the Dutch, who fought to control them; see the spice trade and the Dutch conquest of Banda.
